A1.title: A Big Earthquake Hit Venezuela
A1.content:
A very big earthquake hit Venezuela. Venezuela is a country in South America. The earthquake happened on June 24, 2026. Many people were hurt.

Two big earthquakes came that day. The first earthquake was a 7.2. The second was bigger — a 7.5. They came only 39 seconds apart. This is very fast. When the earth shakes this hard, buildings fall down.

Many buildings fell in Venezuela. Houses, schools, and shops broke and fell. People were inside the buildings. Some people could not get out. They were trapped under the rocks and walls.

More than 1,450 people died. About 3,150 people got hurt. Many more people are missing. Their families do not know where they are. This makes people very sad. Some families are looking for their loved ones every day.

Help came from many places. More than 2,000 rescue workers came to Venezuela. They came from 27 different countries. That is a lot of countries working together. They brought special tools to move big rocks. They also brought 140 rescue dogs. Dogs can use their nose to find people. They can smell people who are under buildings. The dogs help find people who are still alive.

The rescue workers work every day and every night. They do not stop. When they find a person alive, it is a happy moment. But the work is very hard and very sad.

The earthquake also did a lot of damage. Roads broke. Bridges fell. Water pipes broke, so many people do not have clean water. Many people do not have food. Many people do not have a home now. They live in tents or outside.

The United Nations sent help to Venezuela. The United Nations is a big group of countries that work together. They sent money, food, and medicine. They also helped plan the rescue work.

The damage is about 6.7 billion US dollars. This is six percent of Venezuela's total money for one year. This is a very large amount.

People around the world are watching the news about Venezuela. They want to help. Many countries sent workers, money, food, and medicine. This shows that people care about each other.

Life in Venezuela is very hard right now. People are sad and scared. But many people are working hard to help. Rescue workers are finding people every day. Doctors are taking care of the sick and hurt people.

After a big earthquake, it takes a long time to fix everything. Buildings must be rebuilt. Roads must be repaired. But first, people need food, water, and a safe place to sleep. The world must keep helping Venezuela for a long time.

This earthquake is one of the biggest in Venezuela's history. The people of Venezuela are strong. With help from the world, they will rebuild their country and their lives.

vocabulary.definition: when the ground shakes very hard and strongly
to save someone who is in danger
when you cannot move or get out of a place
harm done to buildings or things
when no one can find a person

A2.title: Europe Is Getting Dangerously Hot
A2.content:
Europe is experiencing a very serious heatwave this summer. A heatwave is when the weather is extremely hot for many days without stopping. This year, temperatures across Europe have broken many historical records.

France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Spain, and Switzerland are some of the countries that are very hot right now. Paris, the capital of France, reached 40.9 degrees Celsius on one day in June. This is the highest temperature Paris has ever had in June. In some parts of southern France, it got as hot as 44.3 degrees Celsius.

The United Kingdom also had its hottest June day in history. The temperature reached 36.4 degrees Celsius on Thursday. This is very unusual for the UK, which normally has cool and rainy weather. Switzerland reached 38 degrees Celsius in the northern city of Basel, setting a new record there.

High temperatures are dangerous for people's health. When it is very hot, people can get sick quickly. Older people and young children are in the most danger. They get sick faster than healthy adults. If people do not drink enough water, their bodies can stop working correctly. Hundreds of people have already died because of this heatwave, from Spain to France.

Doctors are giving important advice. They say: drink a lot of water every day, even if you do not feel thirsty. Stay inside where it is cool during the hottest hours. Do not go outside between noon and four in the afternoon, when the sun is strongest. Wear light, loose clothes. Check on elderly neighbors and family members.

The heatwave is also causing problems for nature. Animals are suffering in the heat. Plants and crops are dying because the soil is too dry. Farmers are losing their harvests. In some areas of Spain and southern France, wildfires have started. Hot and dry weather makes it very easy for fires to spread quickly across forests.

This heatwave started in western Europe and is now moving east. Countries like Poland, Hungary, and Romania are getting much hotter. Forecasters say the extreme heat is expected to continue for at least several more days.

Climate scientists say heatwaves like this one are becoming more common every decade. Climate change is making summers hotter around the world. Every year, more temperature records are broken. Scientists warn that countries must work together to reduce pollution and slow climate change, or these events will become more frequent and more deadly.

Governments across Europe are responding. Many cities have opened cool centers in public buildings like libraries and schools where anyone can come to cool down. Some train systems have slowed down because metal rails become dangerously soft in extreme heat. Hospitals are preparing for more patients.

Despite the difficulties, communities across Europe are helping each other. Neighbors are checking on older people who live alone. Local organizations are distributing free water bottles. Europe is facing a serious challenge, but people are working together to protect the most vulnerable.

vocabulary.definition: a long period of unusually hot weather
the highest or most extreme measurement ever officially noted
a dangerous condition when the body loses too much water
a large, uncontrolled fire that burns forests or open land
long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns, largely caused by human activity

B1.title: The Fragile US-Iran Ceasefire Under Pressure
B1.content:
A ceasefire between the United States and Iran is in serious trouble just two weeks after it was signed. The two countries agreed to stop fighting on June 17, 2026, but the agreement is already being violated, and both sides are making strong threats that could lead to a return of full-scale conflict.

The conflict between the US and Iran began earlier this year and involved fighting over the Strait of Hormuz, an important waterway through which about one-fifth of the world's oil supply passes every day. When the war started, oil prices rose sharply, causing economic pain for countries around the world. The ceasefire gave hope that the strait would reopen and global energy supplies would stabilize.

However, the situation deteriorated rapidly this past weekend. Iran struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, directly violating the ceasefire agreement. In response, US and Iranian forces exchanged strikes. US President Donald Trump warned that Iran 'will no longer exist' if the attacks continue. Iran's government threatened to halt all negotiations. These developments have made many international observers very concerned.

Despite the tensions, there are some diplomatic signals worth noting. Iranian officials confirmed that six billion dollars of a total twelve billion in Iranian funds that were frozen in Qatar will be released and returned to Iran. This is an agreed part of the broader diplomatic process. Negotiations have not officially ended, though they are under serious strain.

The conflict is also expanding into new areas. Israel reported a sharp increase in cyberattacks linked to Iran. Israeli authorities recorded about 1,600 hostile cyber incidents last June, but that number has risen to approximately 4,800 cases this month alone. This suggests that even while ceasefire talks continue in the diplomatic sphere, confrontation is continuing through electronic warfare.

Many analysts believe that both sides genuinely want to avoid a full resumption of hostilities. The United States has already spent twenty-nine billion dollars on the conflict. Iran's economy has suffered heavily from international sanctions and wartime disruptions. The cost of continued fighting is high for both sides. Yet trust between the two governments remains very low, and domestic political pressures on both sides make compromise difficult.

The international community is watching nervously. Countries in Asia, including Japan, South Korea, and India, depend heavily on oil that passes through the Strait of Hormuz. Any renewed blockade of the strait could cause serious economic disruption across the region and beyond.

The United Nations and several European governments have called on both sides to exercise restraint and return to serious negotiations. They argue that the ceasefire, despite its imperfections, is far better than the alternative of renewed warfare.

The next few days will be critical. If the two sides can manage the current violations without further escalation, there may still be a realistic path toward a more durable agreement. However, if the situation continues to worsen, the region could face consequences that extend well beyond the two countries directly involved.

vocabulary.definition: a temporary agreement between opposing parties to stop fighting
a narrow body of water connecting two larger seas or oceans
economic or political penalties imposed on a country to pressure it to change its behavior
formal discussions between parties with the goal of reaching an agreement
a gradual increase in the severity or intensity of a conflict

B2.title: Japan Confronts China Over Coast Guard Activity Near Taiwan's Doorstep
B2.content:
Japan has formally lodged a diplomatic protest against Chinese coast guard operations near Yonaguni Island, escalating maritime tensions in one of Asia's most strategically sensitive corridors. Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru publicly declared the activity 'unacceptable,' marking one of Tokyo's strongest verbal responses to Chinese maritime assertiveness in recent memory.

Yonaguni Island, Japan's westernmost territory, sits approximately 110 kilometers from Taiwan's eastern coast. Its location at the edge of Japan's Ryukyu island chain places it directly along sea routes that would be critical in any military contingency involving Taiwan. The island hosts a Japanese Self-Defense Force radar installation, reflecting its recognized strategic importance in monitoring regional military activity.

China's coast guard presence near Yonaguni fits into a broader pattern of assertive maritime behavior that Beijing has pursued across the East and South China Seas in recent years. Chinese authorities regularly justify such operations by referencing their expansive territorial claims, which overlap significantly with the exclusive economic zones of neighboring states. Tokyo, along with Washington and several European capitals, regards these activities as deliberate pressure designed to normalize Chinese maritime dominance before formal territorial disputes are resolved through international mechanisms.

The timing of this incident carries particular geopolitical weight. With American attention partly absorbed by the ongoing and fragile US-Iran ceasefire, analysts have suggested that Beijing may be seizing a moment of relative Western distraction to test Tokyo's responses and reinforce its presence in strategically important waters. This interpretation aligns with a broader pattern in which China has tended to intensify assertive activities during periods when the United States is managing other crises.

For Taiwan, developments near Yonaguni are closely monitored. Although Taipei and Tokyo maintain unofficial but substantive ties — including defense-relevant information sharing — Taiwan cannot formally coordinate with Japan on security responses. Any shift in the maritime balance near Yonaguni directly affects the approaches to Taiwan's eastern coast, traditionally considered the island's most defensible flank.

Japan's protest arrives as Tokyo accelerates a historic defense expansion. Following a landmark decision to double defense spending over five years, Japan has been investing significantly in the defense of its southwestern island chain, including reinforced radar and missile defense capabilities on Yonaguni and neighboring islands. The coast guard incident will likely reinforce political support for these expenditures within Japan's parliament.

Broader multilateral dimensions are also at play. Several Western nations have been conducting freedom-of-navigation operations in contested Asian waters to affirm the principle that international law, not unilateral claims, governs maritime access. Japan's formal protest aligns itself with this position, signaling that Tokyo regards its territorial waters as a matter of legal right rather than negotiable political interest.

The fundamental challenge for Japan is navigating a relationship with China that is simultaneously its largest bilateral trade relationship and its most significant security concern. Any response to Chinese maritime assertiveness must be calibrated to defend national interests without unnecessarily destabilizing an economic interdependence that underpins substantial portions of Japan's export economy. Whether Japan can sustain this balance while also strengthening its defense posture will be one of the defining foreign policy questions of the coming years.

vocabulary.definition: the supreme authority of a state to govern its own territory without external interference
behaving in a confident, forceful manner, especially to advance one's interests or position
a possible future event or situation that requires advance planning
involving three or more countries or parties
the internationally recognized right of ships to travel through international waters without interference

C1.title: Venezuela Earthquake: International Solidarity Meets Systemic Challenges
C1.content:
The twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on June 24, 2026 — magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5, separated by a mere 39 seconds — have precipitated one of the most severe humanitarian crises in Latin American history in recent decades. With the confirmed death toll approaching 1,500, more than 3,150 injured, and tens of thousands still unaccounted for, the scale of devastation forces a reckoning with both Venezuela's systemic infrastructural vulnerabilities and the limits of international emergency response capacity.

The United Nations has coordinated a multilateral rescue effort of considerable scale, deploying 2,245 specialists and 140 search-and-rescue dogs from 44 international USAR teams representing 27 countries. This mobilization stands among the largest internationally coordinated disaster responses of recent years. Yet despite the impressive scope of this deployment, the estimated economic damage of $6.7 billion — equivalent to roughly six percent of Venezuela's annual GDP — makes clear that recovery will be a years-long undertaking extending far beyond emergency search operations.

Venezuela's pre-existing economic fragility significantly compounds the earthquake's impact. Prolonged economic mismanagement, hyperinflation, and the sustained erosion of public infrastructure had already left large segments of the population in precarious conditions before the disaster struck. Many of the structures that collapsed were poorly constructed or inadequately maintained, raising difficult questions about regulatory failures and urban planning deficits that long predated the seismic events themselves. For many Venezuelans, the earthquake did not merely destroy homes — it obliterated the fragile material foundations they had painstakingly preserved through years of economic hardship and political instability.

The political dimensions of the relief effort merit careful scrutiny. Venezuela's government, which has historically maintained adversarial postures toward Western governments and international financial institutions, now finds itself dependent on precisely the multilateral networks it once sought to marginalize. How authorities manage incoming international assistance — whether ensuring equitable distribution to affected communities or channeling it through patronage networks for political advantage — will critically determine recovery outcomes across different regions.

International actors face parallel operational challenges. Delivering aid efficiently within Venezuela's complex political environment requires sustained diplomatic engagement alongside logistical expertise. Organizations experienced in operating in politically sensitive contexts must navigate bureaucratic obstacles and security concerns while maintaining the neutrality and transparency that effective humanitarian response demands.

The Venezuelan crisis also arrives at a moment when global humanitarian response capacity is already stretched by simultaneous crises — ongoing Middle East conflict, economic disruption caused by Europe's record heatwave, and the tail ends of several prior disasters. Donor fatigue presents a genuine risk: sustaining political and financial commitment to Venezuela over months and years, rather than merely the initial days of media attention, will require deliberate advocacy and institutional follow-through from major contributing governments.

Ultimately, the Venezuelan earthquake serves as a stark reminder that seismic resilience — or its profound absence — reflects decisions accumulated across generations: about building standards, urban planning priorities, investment in public infrastructure, and the political will to enforce safety regulations even when doing so conflicts with short-term economic or political interests. Venezuela's path to recovery will be long and uncertain, but the quality of that recovery will be shaped as much by the political choices of its leaders and international partners as by the geological forces that initiated the crisis.

vocabulary.definition: to cause something to happen suddenly or before it would naturally occur
dangerously unstable or uncertain; dependent on circumstances beyond one's control
support or preferential treatment given to individuals based on political loyalty rather than merit
a decline in charitable giving to ongoing crises as public and institutional attention wanes over time
the capacity of structures and communities to withstand and recover from earthquake damage

C2.title: The Unraveling Ceasefire: US-Iran Tensions and the Architecture of Fragile Peace
C2.content:
Barely a fortnight after its signing, the US-Iran ceasefire of June 17, 2026 is exhibiting precisely the pathologies that strategic analysts had long predicted would afflict any agreement forged under military duress between two deeply adversarial states with profoundly asymmetric interests and incompatible frameworks for interpreting the conflict's legitimacy. Iran's strike on a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz — the very waterway whose security the ceasefire was principally designed to guarantee — has exposed the fundamental contradiction at the agreement's core: both parties sought a cessation of hostilities, yet neither has relinquished the strategic objectives that originally drove them into open confrontation.

For the United States, the ceasefire offered an opportunity to arrest the mounting financial hemorrhage of a conflict that has already consumed $29 billion while extricating the administration from a posture of military overextension at a moment when domestic political vulnerabilities — most acutely, voter sensitivity to energy prices and broader economic anxiety ahead of midterm elections — are growing more acute. For Iran, the ceasefire represented a tactical interlude rather than a genuine concession: a breathing space to reconstitute degraded capabilities, extract tangible financial relief (six of a promised twelve billion dollars in frozen Qatari assets are being released), and systematically probe the boundaries of American resolve without crossing thresholds that would compel a full-scale military response.

The agreement's structural deficiencies are now fully manifest. Neither party has consented to credible verification mechanisms, and the absence of a genuinely neutral monitoring body means that disputes over alleged violations are adjudicated unilaterally by parties whose interpretive frameworks are inevitably self-serving. President Trump's warning that Iran 'will no longer exist' if attacks continue exemplifies his characteristic rhetorical maximalism, but it simultaneously constrains US diplomatic flexibility by publicly narrowing the space available for face-saving de-escalation — a dynamic that Iranian negotiators are almost certainly calculating and exploiting.

The concurrent surge in Iranian-attributed cyberattacks on Israel — from approximately 1,600 documented incidents last June to roughly 4,800 cases this month — illuminates a second critical dynamic: the conflict has not ceased but rather migrated into domains where attribution, while plausible, remains formally deniable and where escalatory thresholds are less clearly delineated. This gray-zone strategy allows Tehran to signal continued strategic defiance and maintain domestic political legitimacy without formally violating ceasefire terms as either party has chosen to define them, exploiting the agreement's carefully constructed definitional ambiguities.

Regionally, the ceasefire's instability carries profound implications that transcend the bilateral relationship. Gulf states — simultaneously dependent on Strait of Hormuz transit for their own hydrocarbon exports and reliant on American security guarantees for their survival — face renewed strategic uncertainty about both Washington's reliability and Tehran's ultimate intentions. Major Asian economies, particularly Japan, South Korea, and India, which collectively account for a disproportionate share of global petroleum demand and whose supply chains were severely disrupted during the initial conflict, are recalibrating contingency frameworks for scenarios that their governments had perhaps prematurely assumed were receding.

The deeper analytical question is whether this ceasefire possesses the structural foundations to evolve from a tactical pause born of mutual exhaustion into a durable diplomatic architecture capable of accommodating the genuine security interests of both parties — or whether it will collapse into renewed hostilities that could prove more destructive than the original conflict, given the precedents now established. Historical evidence offers scant grounds for optimism: agreements negotiated from positions of mutual strategic frustration rather than genuine mutual interest carry inherently limited shelf lives, particularly when domestic political incentives on both sides reward intransigence over compromise. What is incontestable is that the next 72 hours will serve as a severe test of whether the leadership of both states retains sufficient strategic discipline to subordinate immediate grievances to long-term interests — a test that, in the current political climate, may prove exceedingly difficult for either side to pass.

vocabulary.definition: characterized by a significant imbalance in power, interests, or capabilities between parties in a relationship or conflict
a severe, uncontrolled outflow — used metaphorically here to describe rapid, unsustainable financial expenditure
the use of ambiguous or deniable actions that fall below conventional thresholds for armed conflict while still achieving strategic objectives
a refusal to compromise or moderate one's position, often despite pressure from others to do so
described or indicated precisely and clearly, leaving no ambiguity about boundaries or scope
